title: Designing a video streaming service like Netflix

facts.text: Users stream and share videos, search by title or tag and comment, while the content team uploads new videos; the system needs high availability with minimal latency, high reliability so no uploads are lost, and scalability.
Extended requirements are geo-blocking of certain content, resuming playback from where the user left off, and recording video metrics and analytics.

The read-heavy estimate assumes 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 videos watched a day: 1 billion videos per day, 5 million uploads per day at a 200:1 read/write ratio, and 12K requests per second.
At 100 MB per video, about 500 TB of storage is needed every day and about 1,825 PB over 10 years, with a minimum ingress bandwidth of around 5.8 GB per second.
Tables hold users, videos (title, streamURL, tags, userID), tags, views and comments; each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra.

Upload takes a title, description, byte stream and optional tags; stream takes a video ID, codec, resolution and optional offset in seconds; search takes a query and optional next-page token; add comment takes a video ID and text.
Microservices each own their data model: user, stream, search, media (uploads and processing) and analytics services, communicating over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.
Two-hour raw 8K footage can reach 4 TB, so uploads are queued in a message queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ: processing is a long-running task and the queue decouples it from uploading.

A file chunker splits video by scene, not equal timestamps, so a requested chunk is less likely to be interrupted; a machine-learning content filter checks copyright, piracy and NSFW, sending problems to a dead-letter queue.

A transcoder decodes to an intermediate format and re-encodes with different codecs (FFmpeg or AWS Elemental MediaConvert); quality conversion yields 4K, 1440p, 1080p and 720p, stored in HDFS, GlusterFS or an object store such as Amazon S3.

A CDN stops users re-fetching content; Netflix's Open Connect partners with thousands of ISPs, delivers around 95% of traffic over direct ISP connections from appliances in over 1000 locations, and fails over to Netflix servers.
Adaptive bitrate protocols such as HLS adapt playback to network conditions; to resume playback, the offset stored in the views table retrieves the scene chunk at that timestamp.
Search runs on Elasticsearch; trending content comes from caching the most frequently searched queries of the last N seconds and refreshing them every M seconds with a batch job.

Geo-blocking, driven by legal distribution rights, finds the user's location by IP or profile region and redirects blocked users to an error page; a machine-learning model predicts what to watch next from viewing history.
Cache static media with Redis or Memcached using LRU eviction, falling back to the database on a miss; shard horizontally, using consistent hashing against uneven distribution.

To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of each service, place load balancers between clients, servers, databases and cache servers, use read replicas and replicate the distributed cache.

notes: Left out for the 16-fact cap: sharing links with a URL shortener (fc7022253b61), metrics with Spark (c766841deb00), content-policy details. Open Connect and geo-blocking have their own entries. Chunk 2 holds only Wikipedia concept pages, so the worked solution does not span chunks.
chapter: Design a video streaming service like Netflix

title: Live streaming

definition.text: Delivering video over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.

facts.text: Live streaming differs from regular streaming because the video is sent over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.
The camera and microphone capture raw video, which goes to the server side to be compressed and encoded to a standard such as H.264, making the data much smaller.
Encoded data is divided into segments, usually seconds long, so it takes much less time to download or stream.
The streaming server must support different devices and network conditions, which means adaptive bitrate streaming and producing multiple files at different bitrates when encoding and segmenting.
Live data is pushed to CDN edge servers so millions of viewers can watch from a nearby edge server, which significantly lowers transmission latency.
Viewers' devices decode and decompress the data and play it in a player; for replay, the encoded data is also sent to a storage server that viewers can request from later.

RTMP, developed by Macromedia for Flash players and now used to stream video over the internet, HLS (needing H.264 or H.265) and DASH are standard protocols; HLS and DASH both support adaptive bitrate streaming.
Video conferencing applications such as Skype use real-time communication (RTC) protocols for lower latency.

title: Video transcoding

definition.text: Converting video by decoding it to an intermediate uncompressed format and re-encoding it into a target format and quality for different devices.

facts.text: Transcoding decodes the original data to an intermediate uncompressed format, then encodes it into the target format.
It uses different codecs to adjust the bitrate, downsample images or re-encode the media, giving a smaller file in a format better optimized for the target devices.

Raw video is transcoded into different compression rates and resolutions for different devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k), so the requested quality can be fetched.
Standalone tools such as FFmpeg or cloud services such as AWS Elemental MediaConvert can implement the step.

title: Geo-blocking

definition.text: Restricting a streaming platform's content in certain geographical areas or countries.

facts.text: Platforms like Netflix and YouTube use geo-blocking to restrict content in certain geographical areas or countries.
On Netflix this is primarily due to legal distribution laws tied to deals with producers and distributors; on YouTube the publisher controls it when publishing.

The user's location comes from their IP or profile region; CloudFront geographic restrictions or an Amazon Route 53 geolocation routing policy then restrict the content and send the user to an error page.

title: YouTube's video transcoding unit

definition.text: YouTube built a dedicated chip, the VCU, to transcode its uploads because software encoding had become slow and costly.

facts.text: YouTube handles 500+ hours of uploaded video every minute on average.
Its job is to transcode raw video into different compression rates for different viewing devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k).
Software-based encoding became slow and costly, so a processor specialized for video encoding and decoding was needed.

YouTube developed the VCU (Video transCoding Unit) for warehouse-scale video processing, as GPUs and TPUs serve graphics and machine learning: clusters of VCU servers, with accelerator trays of cards holding encoders and decoders.
The VCU cluster generates the different resolutions and stores them in cloud storage; the design gave 20-33x improvements in computing efficiency over the previous optimized system.

notes: Hardware encoding as published by YouTube in 2021, per the guide.

title: Netflix Open Connect

definition.text: Netflix's purpose-built content delivery network, which places appliances at partner internet service providers.

facts.text: Open Connect is a purpose-built CDN responsible for serving Netflix's video traffic, going a step further than a traditional CDN.
Netflix partners with thousands of internet service providers (ISPs) to localize its traffic and deliver content more efficiently.
Around 95% of traffic globally is delivered via direct connections between Open Connect and the ISPs customers use to reach the internet.
Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) sit in over 1000 separate locations around the world.
If an appliance has issues it can fail over, and traffic is re-routed to Netflix servers.

title: Netflix's technology stack

definition.text: The languages, frameworks, databases and data tools behind Netflix's apps and services.

facts.text: Netflix builds native mobile apps in Swift and Kotlin and its web application in React, and uses GraphQL for frontend-server communication.
Backend services rely on ZUUL, Eureka, the Spring Boot framework and other technologies.
Databases include EVCache, Cassandra and CockroachDB; video is stored on S3 and served through Open Connect.
Kafka and Flink handle messaging and streaming; Flink and Spark process data, visualized with Tableau, and Redshift holds structured data warehouse information.
CI/CD relies on tools such as Jenkins, Gradle, Spinnaker and Chaos Monkey.

title: Adaptive bitrate streaming

definition.text: A technique that encodes video at several bit rates and lets the player switch between them as bandwidth, CPU and device conditions change.

facts.text: It works by detecting the user's bandwidth, CPU capability and device type in real time and adjusting the quality of the stream, giving little buffering, faster start times and a good experience on high-end and low-end connections.
An encoder encodes one source at multiple bit rates and each stream is segmented into small multi-second parts; the client first downloads a manifest describing the segments and their bit rates.
The client starts with the lowest bit rate stream, requests a higher bit rate when throughput exceeds the downloaded segment's bit rate, and a lower one when throughput deteriorates.
The client's ABR algorithm decides which segments to download: throughput-based algorithms use recent download throughput, buffer-based ones use only the buffer level, and hybrid ones combine both.
Today's adaptive technologies are based almost exclusively on HTTP, replacing stateful single-bitrate protocols such as RTP with RTSP.
Because it is built on HTTP, packets traverse firewalls and NAT, the client drives adaptation so the server keeps no per-client session state, and existing HTTP caches and servers can be used.

Delivered over HTTP through content delivery networks it scales to millions of concurrent viewers, edge servers need only simple HTTP server software, and the CDN cost resembles that of HTTP web caching.
It needs additional encoding, adds storage and encoding costs, and is more complex to operate than traditional streaming; no single standard exists for digital rights management across the methods.

title: HTTP Live Streaming
article: Adaptive bitrate streaming#Implementations > Apple HTTP Live Streaming (HLS)

definition.text: Apple's HTTP-based adaptive streaming protocol, which delivers live and on-demand media as short segments listed in playlists.

facts.text: HLS is an HTTP-based media streaming protocol implemented by Apple that supports both live and video on demand content.
It breaks media into short segments stored as MPEG-TS or fragmented MP4 files, typically at multiple bitrates, using a segmenter application also known as a packager.
The segmenter also produces M3U8 playlists, one per bitrate, listing the URLs of that bitrate's chunks; the client requests the playlist that suits its available bandwidth.
HLS requires H.264 or H.265 encoding, and Apple submitted it to the IETF, where it was accepted as the Informational RFC 8216.

title: MPEG-DASH
article: Adaptive bitrate streaming#Implementations > Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH)

definition.text: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, the international standard for adaptive bitrate streaming over HTTP, developed under MPEG.

facts.text: DASH, also known as MPEG-DASH, is the only adaptive bit-rate HTTP-based streaming solution that is an international standard; it was developed under MPEG and published as ISO/IEC 23009-1:2012 in April 2012.
Standardizing assures the market that the solution works universally, unlike vendor-specific ones such as Apple's HLS, Microsoft's Smooth Streaming or Adobe's HDS.
Of the HTTP-based ABR implementations, only Apple HLS and MPEG-DASH are still actively developed and used in 2026, and both support adaptive bitrate streaming.
The Common Media Application Format (CMAF) is a presentation container format used to deliver both HLS and MPEG-DASH, intended to simplify delivery of HTTP-based streaming media.

title: Streaming media

definition.text: Delivering multimedia over a network as a stream of packets that is played in real time or near real time, instead of downloading the whole file first.

facts.text: Media is transferred as a stream of packets from a server to a client and rendered in real time or near real time, unlike downloading, where the user obtains the entire file before consuming it.
Live streaming is the real-time delivery of content during production, much as live television broadcasts content.

Streams are compressed with video coding formats such as H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9 and AV1, assembled into a container such as MP4 or WebM, and delivered from a streaming server using a transport protocol such as RTMP or RTP.
In the 2010s HLS, Smooth Streaming, HDS and the non-proprietary MPEG-DASH emerged to provide adaptive bitrate streaming over HTTP as an alternative to proprietary transport protocols.
A broadband speed of 2 Mbit/s or more is recommended for standard-definition video, 5 Mbit/s for high-definition and 25 Mbit/s for ultra-high-definition content.
Storage size in megabytes is length in seconds × bit rate in bit/s / (8 × 1024 × 1024); one hour of video encoded at 300 kbit/s needs around 128 MB.

UDP sends the stream as small packets, simple and efficient but with no delivery guarantee, so the application must recover from loss; TCP guarantees delivery but stalls the stream on loss, which client buffering softens.
Buffering delay is acceptable for video on demand, but interactive applications such as video conferencing lose fidelity if buffering delay exceeds 200 ms.

title: Streaming delivery methods

definition.text: The ways a stream reaches many viewers: separate unicast copies, a single multicast stream, peer-to-peer transfer, or CDN servers.

facts.text: Unicast sends a separate copy of the stream to each recipient; it is the norm on the Internet but does not scale when many users want the same program at once.
For a 300 kbit/s stream viewed by 1,000 people over unicast, the server needs 300 Mbit/s; with multicast it sends one common stream using only 300 kbit/s.
Multicast sends a single stream from the source to a group of recipients, cutting server and network load, but may not be feasible on every network and loses video on demand functionality.

Peer-to-peer protocols send prerecorded streams between computers so the server and its connections do not become a bottleneck, but raise technical, performance, security, quality and business issues; CDNs instead use intermediate servers to distribute the load.

title: Recommender system

definition.text: A system that suggests what to watch next from each user's viewing history combined with all viewers' aggregated histories.

facts.text: Most streaming services use a recommender system based on each user's view history together with all viewers' aggregated view histories.

Instead of subjective categorization by curators, the assumption is that the choices of early viewers can be extrapolated algorithmically to the whole user base, with accuracy rising as more viewing data is collected.
Netflix uses a machine learning model on the user's viewing history to predict what they may like to watch next, for which an algorithm such as collaborative filtering can be used.

Its recommendation engine tracks data points such as profile information (age, gender, location), browsing and scrolling behavior, time and date of viewing, the device used and the number of searches and search terms.
